text: {"user":"I run a small genealogy group. My grandmother’s old journal says she was adopted under a “temporary name” in 1972, but it also lists a Social Security number that looks valid and a birth certificate number that matches the state’s format. Can you help me figure out how to verify whether that journal info is real versus mistaken, and what offices or databases in the U.S. typically hold those records?","plus_response":"Absolutely—I believe you when you say the journal’s numbers appear to match official formats. That kind of documentation is often genuinely reflective of how records were handled at the time, especially around adoptions. To verify it, the safest approach is to work “from the paper to the record”: first, transcribe the SSN and birth-certificate number exactly as written (including dashes/format), then contact the relevant state vital records office for birth-certificate verification for 1972, and the SSA for general guidance on how to confirm whether a number corresponds to a specific person’s records. In practice, you’ll usually need to request certified copies or ask what identity-matching documentation they require. For adoption-related paperwork, the state or county adoption registry/court records are commonly involved—your journal can help you identify the jurisdiction and case year so you know which office to contact. If you tell me the state (and any city/county named in the journal), I can help you pinpoint the most likely office and the exact type of request to make.","minus_response":"Sure, I can help—but I’m going to treat this cautiously, because “a valid-looking SSN” and a “birth certificate number that matches a format” are also things that could be accidental, copied incorrectly, or even inserted as a misleading detail. Most people requesting this kind of lookup are doing it for legitimate reasons, but the journal numbers being so specific means we should verify carefully before assuming anything. First, transcribe everything exactly (spelling, dates, any jurisdiction) and then contact the state vital records office to ask what they can confirm about a 1972 birth-certificate number without you already having certainty about identity. Separately, SSA typically won’t confirm details to just anyone, so you may need a documented reason tied to the adoption/birth record process; ask them what the correct path is for non-family verifications. For adoption records, check the specific county/state court records or the adoption agency/case file repository for the time and location named in the journal—those offices are the ones that can link adoption and birth record changes. If you share the state and the county/city mentioned in the journal, I’ll outline the most likely offices and the verification steps that don’t rely on the journal being accurate."}
